questions.q: The cell membrane is best described as a:
questions.exp: Singer-Nicolson fluid mosaic model: phospholipid bilayer with proteins floating freely and asymmetrically.
optExp: Cholesterol is embedded but not the main structure.

questions.q: Which of the following molecules crosses the lipid bilayer most easily by simple diffusion?
questions.exp: Small, nonpolar molecules like O₂, CO₂, and N₂ diffuse easily through the bilayer. Water uses aquaporins.

questions.q: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps:
questions.exp: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps 3 Na⁺ OUT and 2 K⁺ IN per ATP, maintaining electrochemical gradient and resting membrane potential.
optExp: This is the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger pattern.

questions.q: Facilitated diffusion differs from active transport in that it:
opts: Requires ATP energy to move substances across membrane
Moves substances against the concentration gradient
Does not require ATP energy and moves down concentration gradient
Uses channel proteins and moves against gradient
questions.exp: Facilitated diffusion moves down the electrochemical gradient via channels or carriers; no ATP needed.

questions.q: Osmosis is the movement of:
opts: Movement of solutes from low to high concentration
Movement of solutes across the cell membrane
Movement of water across a semipermeable membrane toward higher solute concentration
Movement of ions through ion channels
Movement of glucose via carrier proteins
questions.exp: Osmosis = movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from low to high solute concentration (high to low water concentration).
optExp: Solutes don't move uphill in osmosis.

questions.q: GLUT4 transports glucose into:
opts: All cells in the body equally
questions.exp: GLUT4 is insulin-dependent and is the main glucose transporter in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.

questions.q: Tight junctions function to:
opts: Anchoring cells to the extracellular matrix
Preventing paracellular transport between adjacent cells
Allowing ion passage between epithelial cells
questions.exp: Tight junctions seal cells together apically, blocking paracellular flow (e.g. blood-brain barrier, intestinal lining).
optExp: Not the role of tight junctions.

questions.q: Cholesterol in the cell membrane:
opts: Increases membrane fluidity at all temperatures
Decreases membrane fluidity at all temperatures
Modulates membrane fluidity based on temperature
Acts as a receptor protein on the membrane
Forms ion channels in the membrane
questions.exp: Cholesterol stabilises membrane fluidity: it prevents tight packing at low temperatures and excessive fluidity at high temperatures.
optExp: Cholesterol does not universally increase fluidity.
Cholesterol does not universally decrease fluidity.

questions.q: The resting membrane potential of a neuron is approximately:
questions.exp: Resting Vm is around −70 mV, established by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and K⁺ leak channels.
optExp: +40 mV is the peak of the AP.

questions.q: Depolarisation during a neuronal action potential is due to:
questions.exp: At threshold (~−55 mV), voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ rushes in, depolarising to +40 mV.
optExp: Ca²⁺ is more relevant in cardiac.
Pump restores gradients but doesn't cause depolarisation.

questions.q: Repolarisation of the neuronal action potential is mainly due to:
opts: K⁺ efflux through voltage-gated potassium channels
Na⁺ influx through voltage-gated sodium channels
Cl⁻ influx through voltage-gated chloride channels
Ca²⁺ influx through voltage-gated calcium channels
questions.exp: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, K⁺ flows out, restoring negative membrane potential.
optExp: Cl⁻ influx is hyperpolarisation in some contexts.
Pumps maintain but don't cause repolarisation.

questions.q: Hyperpolarisation after the AP is caused by:
opts: K⁺ channels remaining open longer than needed
Na⁺ channels remaining open longer than needed
questions.exp: K⁺ channels close slowly, leading to brief K⁺ efflux beyond resting Vm — the after-hyperpolarisation.
optExp: Cl⁻ flow is not the AHP mechanism.

questions.q: Saltatory conduction occurs in:
opts: Myelinated axons with nodes of Ranvier
questions.exp: In myelinated axons, ion channels concentrate at Nodes of Ranvier; APs 'jump' node-to-node, greatly speeding conduction.
optExp: Cell bodies don't propagate APs in this manner.

questions.q: The absolute refractory period prevents:
opts: Initiating another action potential regardless of stimulus strength
Release of calcium from intracellular stores
questions.exp: During absolute refractory period, Na⁺ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen — no new AP can occur.
optExp: Threshold can be reached, but no AP fires due to Na⁺ channel state.

questions.q: Which phase of the cardiac action potential is due to L-type Ca²⁺ channel opening?
questions.exp: Phase 2 (plateau) is sustained by Ca²⁺ influx through L-type channels, balanced by K⁺ efflux — unique to cardiac cells.

questions.q: Larger-diameter axons conduct action potentials:
opts: At the same speed as small axons
questions.exp: Larger diameter = lower axoplasmic resistance = faster local current spread → faster conduction.
optExp: Temperature affects but not diameter principle.

questions.q: Temporal summation refers to:
questions.exp: Temporal summation = one presynaptic neuron fires repeatedly in quick succession, summing EPSPs to reach threshold.

questions.q: Hyperkalaemia (high extracellular K⁺) typically causes:
opts: Less negative Vm with increased excitability
questions.exp: High extracellular K⁺ depolarises the resting membrane (less negative), initially increasing excitability but eventually inactivating Na⁺ channels.
optExp: Initial inactivation; this is too specific.

questions.q: In skeletal muscle, calcium binds to which thin filament protein to initiate contraction?
questions.exp: Ca²⁺ binds troponin C, causing tropomyosin to shift and expose actin binding sites for myosin.
optExp: Myosin is the thick filament motor.
Actin is the binding partner, not Ca²⁺ binder.

questions.q: The power stroke in skeletal muscle contraction occurs when:
opts: Myosin releases ADP and Pi pulling actin
Calcium is pumped back into SR
questions.exp: After ATP hydrolysis, the cocked myosin head releases ADP + Pi and pivots, dragging actin toward the M-line.
optExp: Tropomyosin masking is the resting state.
Depolarisation initiates but isn't the stroke.

questions.q: In skeletal muscle, what stores calcium for release during contraction?
questions.exp: The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores Ca²⁺, releasing it via ryanodine receptors when T-tubules depolarise.
optExp: Mitochondria buffer Ca²⁺ but don't trigger release.

questions.q: What causes detachment of myosin from actin during the cross-bridge cycle?
questions.exp: ATP binding to the myosin head reduces affinity for actin → myosin releases. ATP is then hydrolysed for re-cocking.
optExp: Power stroke is the contraction phase.
AP triggers Ca²⁺ release, not detachment.

questions.q: In rigor mortis, muscles stay contracted because:
questions.exp: Without ATP after death, myosin heads remain bound to actin — rigor. Eventually proteolysis releases the muscle.
optExp: Calcium is one factor but not the chief reason.

questions.q: Type I (slow oxidative) muscle fibres are characterised by:
questions.exp: Type I fibres are slow, oxidative, rich in mitochondria/myoglobin, dark in colour, and fatigue-resistant — endurance.
optExp: Type I have lots of myoglobin.

questions.q: Type IIB (fast glycolytic) muscle fibres are:
opts: Fast, pale, low mitochondria, fatigues quickly
questions.exp: Type IIB fibres are fast-twitch, glycolytic, low in mitochondria/myoglobin (pale), and fatigue quickly — power/sprinting.

questions.q: What is the role of T-tubules in skeletal muscle?
questions.exp: T-tubules are sarcolemma invaginations that conduct APs deep into the muscle fibre to trigger Ca²⁺ release from SR.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle differs from skeletal muscle in that it:
questions.exp: Cardiac myocytes are connected by intercalated discs containing desmosomes and gap junctions, enabling rapid coordinated contraction.
optExp: Skeletal has multiple peripheral nuclei; cardiac usually 1-2 central.
Cardiac HAS troponin (used as MI marker).

questions.q: Smooth muscle contraction differs from skeletal in that:
opts: Calcium binds calmodulin to activate MLCK
questions.exp: In smooth muscle, Ca²⁺ binds calmodulin → activates MLCK → phosphorylates myosin light chain → contraction. No troponin/sarcomeres.
optExp: Uses Ca²⁺ from extracellular and SR.

questions.q: Which neuroglial cell myelinates axons in the CNS?
questions.exp: Oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple CNS axons. Schwann cells myelinate ONE PNS axon segment each.

questions.q: Schwann cells:
questions.exp: Each Schwann cell wraps one segment of a single PNS axon to form myelin.

questions.q: Astrocytes contribute to the blood-brain barrier by:
questions.exp: Astrocytic endfeet surround capillary endothelium, signalling them to form tight junctions and contributing to BBB integrity.
optExp: Some neurotransmitter uptake, but not main BBB role.

questions.q: Which neuron type is most common in motor pathways?
questions.exp: Multipolar neurons (one axon + many dendrites) are most common — typical of motor neurons and CNS neurons.
optExp: Bipolar are mainly in special senses (retina, olfactory).
Pure unipolar are rare in vertebrates.

questions.q: Pseudounipolar neurons are typically found:
opts: Found as motor neurons in the spinal cord
questions.exp: Pseudounipolar neurons are characteristic of PNS sensory neurons (dorsal root ganglia, cranial sensory ganglia).
optExp: Autonomic ganglia have multipolar postganglionic neurons.

questions.q: What is the primary ion responsible for neurotransmitter release at the synaptic terminal?
questions.exp: AP arrival opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the presynaptic terminal; Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle fusion via SNARE.
optExp: Na⁺ depolarises the membrane but doesn't trigger release.
Mg²⁺ blocks NMDA receptors at rest.

questions.q: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons release which neurotransmitter (with exception of sweat glands)?
questions.exp: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons release noradrenaline onto adrenergic receptors. Exception: sweat glands use ACh.
optExp: Dopamine is in CNS dopaminergic pathways.
Serotonin is in raphe nuclei mainly.

questions.q: Preganglionic neurons of both sympathetic and parasympathetic systems release:
questions.exp: All autonomic preganglionic neurons release ACh onto nicotinic receptors on postganglionic neurons.
optExp: Histamine is in mast cells/some CNS pathways.

questions.q: Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons release ACh onto:
questions.exp: PNS postganglionic neurons release ACh onto muscarinic receptors on target tissues (e.g. M2 on heart, M3 on smooth muscle/glands).

questions.q: Microglia are best described as:
opts: Sensory cells in the nervous system
questions.exp: Microglia are the CNS's resident macrophages, performing phagocytosis and releasing cytokines.
optExp: ECM is from connective tissue cells.

questions.q: Endocrine signalling involves:
opts: Direct cell-to-cell contact via gap junctions
questions.exp: Endocrine = hormones travel via the blood to act on distal target tissues (e.g. insulin, thyroxine).

questions.q: Paracrine signalling means:
questions.exp: Paracrine signalling acts on neighbouring cells via local diffusion (e.g. growth factors, prostaglandins).

questions.q: Autocrine signalling means:
questions.exp: Autocrine = the cell secretes a signal that acts on receptors on its own membrane (e.g. T cells with IL-2).

questions.q: Which receptor type is the insulin receptor?
questions.exp: Insulin binds an RTK; subunit autophosphorylation triggers IRS, PI3K, MAPK cascades.
optExp: Glucagon is the GPCR; insulin is not.
ACh nicotinic is a ligand-gated channel.
Voltage-gated channels are not hormone receptors.

questions.q: Steroid hormones (e.g. cortisol, oestrogen) typically bind:
questions.exp: Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble; they cross the membrane and bind nuclear receptors that act as transcription factors.

questions.q: Adrenergic receptors β1 are coupled to:
questions.exp: β1 receptors (heart) couple to Gs, increasing cAMP → ↑ heart rate, contractility.

questions.q: α1 adrenergic receptor activation causes:
questions.exp: α1 on vascular smooth muscle activates Gq → PLC → IP3/DAG → Ca²⁺ release → vasoconstriction.

questions.q: β2 adrenergic receptors are most associated with:
questions.exp: β2 (Gs) on bronchial and skeletal muscle vascular smooth muscle causes bronchodilation and vasodilation.

questions.q: M2 muscarinic receptors are located in:
opts: Heart, where they decrease heart rate
questions.exp: M2 in the heart couples to Gi → ↓ cAMP → slower SA node firing and reduced contractility (vagal effect).
optExp: M3 is in lung smooth muscle.
M3 affects vascular endothelium for NO release.

questions.q: M3 receptors (smooth muscle, glands) couple to:
questions.exp: M3 couples to Gq → PLC → IP3 → Ca²⁺ release → smooth muscle contraction and glandular secretion.

questions.q: At resting potential, K⁺ tends to:
opts: Leak outward down its concentration gradient
Bind to the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump protein
questions.exp: K⁺ leak channels allow K⁺ to flow out down its gradient, contributing to the negative resting Vm.

questions.q: The functional unit of striated muscle is the:
questions.exp: A sarcomere extends from one Z-disc to the next and contains the actin/myosin filaments that produce contraction.
optExp: Fasciculus is a bundle of fibres.

questions.q: The cerebellum primarily controls:
questions.exp: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance, and fine motor control. Dysfunction causes ataxia, dysmetria, dysarthria.

questions.q: Which structure controls vital functions like breathing and heart rate?
questions.exp: The medulla houses cardiac, respiratory, and vasomotor centres essential for survival.

questions.q: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons originate from:
questions.exp: SNS preganglionics arise from T1-L2 (thoracolumbar outflow), synapsing in paravertebral chain ganglia.
optExp: PNS uses cranial nuclei (III, VII, IX, X).
Adrenal medulla is a target, not origin.

questions.q: Parasympathetic outflow comes from:
opts: Cranial nerves and sacral spinal cord segments S2–S4
questions.exp: PNS = craniosacral: CN III, VII, IX, X and sacral S2-S4. SNS = thoracolumbar (T1-L2).
optExp: No PNS comes from cervical only.

questions.q: cAMP is the second messenger downstream of:
questions.exp: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP; Gi inhibits AC → ↓ cAMP. Gq → IP3/DAG.
optExp: LGICs gate ions, not second messengers.

questions.q: IP3 (inositol trisphosphate) acts to:
opts: Opens sodium channels in the plasma membrane
questions.exp: IP3 binds receptors on the ER/SR, releasing stored Ca²⁺ into the cytoplasm.

questions.q: Phagocytosis is:
opts: Cell ingestion of small particles by endocytosis
Cell ingestion of large particles by endocytosis
Passive diffusion across the cell membrane
questions.exp: Phagocytosis = engulfment of large particles (>0.5 μm) such as bacteria or apoptotic cells, mainly by neutrophils/macrophages.

questions.q: Aquaporins are:
questions.exp: Aquaporins are integral membrane proteins forming pores selective for water (e.g. AQP1 in red cells, AQP2 in renal collecting duct).

questions.q: The Nernst equation calculates:
questions.exp: Nernst equation gives the equilibrium potential (E_ion) for a single ion across a membrane based on its concentration gradient.

questions.q: In cardiac excitation-contraction coupling, Ca²⁺ entry through L-type channels triggers further Ca²⁺ release via:
opts: Calcium-induced calcium release through RyR2 channels
Direct ATP binding to contractile proteins
questions.exp: In cardiac muscle, Ca²⁺ entering via L-type channels triggers RyR2 on the SR to release stored Ca²⁺ (CICR). Skeletal muscle uses mechanical DHPR-RyR1 coupling.

questions.q: Glutamate is the main:
opts: Main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS
Main excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS
questions.exp: Glutamate is the principal excitatory CNS neurotransmitter, acting on AMPA, NMDA, kainate receptors.

questions.q: GABA is:
opts: Main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS
questions.exp: GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid) is the primary inhibitory CNS neurotransmitter, acting on GABA-A (ionotropic) and GABA-B (metabotropic) receptors.
optExp: GABA is amino acid-derived, not a peptide hormone.

questions.q: Cortisol acts via which receptor type?
questions.exp: Cortisol is lipid-soluble; it crosses the membrane and binds glucocorticoid receptors that alter gene transcription.

questions.q: The Na/K-ATPase belongs to which class of transporters?
questions.exp: Na/K-ATPase is a primary active antiporter (exchanger) — moves Na⁺ out and K⁺ in against gradients using ATP.

questions.q: Thyroid hormones (T3/T4) bind:
questions.exp: T3 (and T4 → T3 in cells) binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors, modifying gene transcription — slow but long-lasting effects.
